title: Goto statements
recap: A goto statement jumps to a labeled statement, forward or backward. A backward jump can replace a loop, but repeated jumps quickly produce spaghetti code that is hard to follow.

Modern C++ prefers loops, break, continue, and functions. Goto remains useful in a few narrow cases, such as jumping to shared cleanup code, and this lesson shows its mechanics so you can recognize it.
objectives: Implement firstSuccessfulAttempt from its behavioral contract.
Practice the lesson construct by writing the control flow yourself.
Handle multiple inputs and edge cases without hard-coded example answers.
warnings: The examples are not the whole test suite; implement the general behavior.
Do not edit the test drivers. Only the supplied public function signatures are fixed.
Console output and exact source tokens are not graded.
challenge: Implement a retry simulation with a backward goto. The first failuresBeforeSuccess attempts fail; the next succeeds. Return the successful attempt number (numbered from 1), or -1 if the attempt budget is exhausted. Negative failures or maxAttempts <= 0 are invalid and return -1. No printing or real network calls. This is a small goto demonstration, not a recommendation to use goto in ordinary retry code.
hints: Validate the inputs before reaching the retry label.
The attempt succeeds when its number is greater than the number of failures.
Stop at the budget; otherwise increment and jump back.
